title: Debt Collection Lawsuits Surge to Pre-Pandemic Highs
pub: The Pew Charitable Trusts — Courts & Communities
author: The Pew Charitable Trusts

dom.t: Self-representation: Cheaper filings may shift institutional costs

mo.t: Justice access: Direct AI use shifts risk downward
Legal workflows: Immediate gains create competence risks
Self-representation: Cheaper filings may shift institutional costs

kp.k: Debt litigation increased across urban and rural courts
kp.d: The September 2, 2025 article reports up to 4.7 million debt collection cases filed in 2022, according to Pew calculations, followed by sharp increases in 2023 and 2024, often exceeding pre-pandemic levels. Nationwide data is not readily available: January Advisors reviewed statewide filings in Minnesota, Missouri, Indiana, North Dakota, Connecticut, and Virginia, alongside major metropolitan areas including Houston, Austin, Dallas, Maricopa County, and Philadelphia.
qs: State courts nationwide are grappling with spikes in debt collection lawsuits, according to two new reports from January Advisors and the National Center for State Courts (NCSC).
The surge observed in debt cases in 2023 and 2024 holds true across both rural and urban areas, including rural North Dakota and densely populated Maricopa.

kp.k: AI-enabled filing is a hypothesis, not established causation
kp.d: Pew reports that NCSC's June report hypothesized AI partly explains rising debt claims by making complaint filing easier for collectors. NCSC found year-over-year increases in contract-case filings of 21% in 2022 and 15% in 2023; this category can include debt, foreclosure, and landlord-tenant cases, so the figures are not debt-only measures. The article reports that other civil case types did not experience the same increases despite similar economic conditions; it does not establish AI's causal contribution.
qs: identified the recent rise in debt claims and hypothesized that it was partially due to artificial intelligence, or AI.
21% in 2022 and 15% in 2023 from the years prior, and pointed to how the use of AI could make filing more complaints easier for debt collectors.
Despite similar economic conditions, all other civil case types did not experience the same increases.

kp.k: Large repeat plaintiffs account for growing docket shares
kp.d: January Advisors' table compares the top 10 plaintiffs' shares of debt cases in 2019 and 2024: Indiana rose from 27.7% to 47.4%, Connecticut from 63.9% to 80.2%, Virginia from 31.4% to 47.4%, Minnesota from 53.2% to 66.4%, Wisconsin from 37.4% to 49.2%, and North Dakota from 66.7% to 67.9%. The table reports relative changes of 71.4%, 25.6%, 50.7%, 24.7%, 31.4%, and 1.9%, respectively. These are aggregate top-filer comparisons, not necessarily the same companies across years. The article also reports a 350% increase in LVNV Funding's filings over that period.
qs: A handful of national companies, such as debt buyers and banks, file the bulk of cases and help account for the recent surge.
The businesses in 2019 may not be exactly the same in 2024 because researchers looked at the aggregate number of filings by the top 10 companies, not the individual companies.
The analysis of these states by January Advisors shows that one national debt buyer in particular—LVNV Funding—increased filings by 350% for the same period.

kp.k: Many debt lawsuits involve relatively small consumer claims
kp.d: For states with available data, including Utah, Minnesota, and Michigan, the article reports that historically about half of debt collection cases concern less than $2,000. Credit card or bank debt and medical debt are identified as the most common sources. These findings describe available state evidence rather than a comprehensive national estimate.
qs: Businesses initiate lawsuits against a consumer for an alleged debt owed.
historically about half of all debt collection cases are for less than $2,000

kp.k: Consumers face litigation overwhelmingly without legal representation
kp.d: The article reports consumer representation in fewer than 10% of cases, with rates as low as 0.6%. It attributes frequent nonparticipation to confusing court processes or lack of understanding about why consumers were sued. This identifies an access-to-justice problem accompanying increased litigation volume, rather than evidence that AI improves consumer access to counsel.
qs: consumers are represented in fewer than 10% of cases (or as low as 0. 6%)
most often do not come to court or participate in the case against them because court processes can be confusing or they may not understand why they have been sued.

kp.k: Claim scrutiny may fail even where legally required
kp.d: Pew states that courts issue judgments without examining the facts when consumers do not participate. It cites studies in Connecticut, California, and Minnesota indicating that officials may fail to review claim validity, the amount owed, or the defendant's identity even when review is required. The recommendation to check cases concerns judicial scrutiny of debt claims, not specifically human verification of AI output.
qs: Courts are left to issue judgments without any examination of the facts.
and Minnesota show that even when required, court officials may not review whether a claim is valid, how much is owed, or whether the right person is being sued.

kp.k: Judgments carry substantial and long-lasting enforcement consequences
kp.d: The article explains that judgments enable garnishment of assets or wages. It reports that debt judgments can persist for at least a decade in 35 states and Washington D.C., with renewal possible in 18 of those jurisdictions if unpaid. These consequences underpin Pew's call for claim-validity checks and policies supporting participation.
qs: Once a court issues a judgment, that judgment carries with it the full enforcement power of the court, including the authority for a business to garnish a consumer’s assets or wages.
for at least a decade—and in 18 of those jurisdictions, a financial judgment can be renewed if not paid off.

kp.k: Pew recommends participation reforms and automatic post-judgment protections
kp.d: Pew recommends removing requirements for written answers or fees to file them, improving and reviewing disclosures, and making post-judgment protections automatic. It distinguishes legislators' authority over governing laws from judges' and administrators' handling of cases. The article presents improved validity, participation, repayment, and equal treatment as potential outcomes of reform, not measured results.
qs: Although court administrators and judges decide how matters before the court should be handled, legislators make the laws that determine the range of issues that can be considered and how cases progress in the system.
removing legal barriers such as requiring written answers or fees to file those answers, improving and reviewing disclosures, and making post-judgment protections automatic.
Implementing such policies can also help more people without attorneys to actively participate in their cases.
If applied nationwide, these reforms could allow more people to pay back their debts and ensure that courts are achieving their vision of equal and fair treatment for all.

cl.s: Concrete claim or prediction about how AI changes legal services, the legal profession, or legal markets (or, for a cross-domain source, its own domain)

pts.k: AI could make it easier for debt collectors to file more complaints and could partly explain rising debt litigation.
pts.d: Pew authors Lester Bird and Casey Chiappetta report an NCSC research hypothesis that AI partly accounts for the recent increase in debt claims by facilitating complaint filing. The proposed causal connection is presented as a hypothesis, not an established finding.

cl.s: Evidence basis offered for the claim (data, benchmarks, cases, experience, authority, or none)

pts.k: The article cites NCSC filing statistics and comparisons across civil case types, rather than direct measurement of AI use.
pts.d: The cited NCSC report records year-on-year increases in contract filings of 21% in 2022 and 15% in 2023. This category includes debt lawsuits, foreclosure, and landlord-tenant cases, so the figures are not specific to debt collection alone. The article also notes that other civil case types did not experience comparable increases despite similar economic conditions. January Advisors' data provides additional context about rising debt filings in selected jurisdictions in 2023 and 2024, but the article does not provide direct evidence linking particular filings or collectors to AI adoption.

cl.s: Stated or implied timeframe, conditions or qualifications under which the claim holds

pts.k: The AI hypothesis concerns recent filing increases, not a forecast with a specified future deadline.
pts.d: Published September 2, 2025, the article refers to an NCSC report released in June and its contract-filing figures for 2022 and 2023. The broader debt-litigation discussion concerns increases in 2023 and 2024. AI is described only as a possible partial explanation; the source neither quantifies its contribution nor specifies when collectors began using it.

cl.s: Who is affected and how (market segment, role, firm type, clients, or the public)

pts.k: Debt collectors may gain easier complaint filing; courts and consumer defendants bear the pressures associated with increased litigation.
pts.d: The direct AI-related claim concerns debt collectors' ability to file more complaints. The article separately describes the broader consequences of rising debt litigation for state courts and consumers, many of whom lack representation: docket congestion, judgments, and potential garnishment. These consequences provide context for the AI hypothesis, but are not demonstrated to result specifically from AI. The source stresses the need to check claim validity and improve participation by unrepresented defendants.
